extracted.intended_audience: employers, employee representatives, HR professionals, labor lawyers, and policymakers involved in FLSA EAP exemption determinations and compliance
extracted.subtask_short: EAP exemption salary and HCE standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards for setting and applying the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) executive/administrative/professional (EAP) standard salary level, the highly compensated employee (HCE) total compensation threshold, the updating mechanism, and severability of provisions. Includes methodological criteria, exclusions, and operational details for determining exemption status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salary level as initial screening function
rubrics_metrics.description: Salary is an important indicator of whether an individual is employed in a bona fide EAP capacity and therefore a key element in defining the exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The salary level should restore and maintain the salary level's "initial screening function"—ensuring that employees who earn below a historically appropriate threshold (e.g., the long test level) are excluded from the exemption. The Department describes the salary level's role as "useful, but limited," and expects duties to remain determinative for many workers between thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard salary level methodology (percentile + region)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the standard salary level equal to the 35th percentile of weekly nonhourly earnings in the lowest-wage Census Region (resulting in $1,128 per week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a percentile in the lowest-wage region (the South) helps account for the shift to a one-test system while reasonably distributing impact and limiting the number of affected workers. The Department intentionally set the salary level below the midpoint between long and short test levels to limit affected workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties test remains determinative for many in salary range
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties will continue to be determinative of exemption status for a majority of white-collar workers earning between applicable salary thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing who is affected by a salary change, agencies and commenters must examine both earnings and duties: not all workers earning below the new salary level will be newly nonexempt because many already fail the duties test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probability codes to determine duties-test outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department applies its probability codes to determine populations of currently exempt workers who meet the standard duties test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department considers these probability codes to be reliable and appropriate indicators of whether an employee meets the standard duties test and has consistently applied this methodology in recent part 541 rules. Commenters challenging affected-worker estimates must offer an alternative methodology at least as robust as the Department's probability codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE test total annual compensation threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: To be exempt under the HCE test, an employee must earn at least the total annual compensation amount specified in the regulations (finalized at $151,164 per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCE threshold is intended to be high enough to reserve the test for employees "at the very top of [the] economic ladder" and to avoid unintended exemptions of employees in high-wage regions and industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE threshold composition requirement (salary/fee basis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the HCE threshold amount, no less than the full standard salary level amount must be paid on a salary or fee basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The remainder of the employee's total annual compensation may include commissions, nondiscretionary bonuses, and other nondiscretionary compensation. Total annual compensation does not include board, lodging, other facilities, or payments for medical insurance, life insurance, retirement plans, or other fringe benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE primary-duty and duties-content requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The employee must "customarily and regularly perform[ ] any one or more of the exempt duties or responsibilities of an executive, administrative, or professional employee."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The HCE test applies only to employees whose primary duty includes performing office or non-manual work. The HCE is a streamlined alternative because very high compensation is a strong indicator an employee will almost invariably pass the standard duties test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-up payment allowance for HCE compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer is permitted to make a final "catch-up" payment during the last pay period or within 1 month after the end of the 52-week period to bring an employee's compensation up to the required level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows employers to ensure total annual compensation meets the HCE threshold even if nondiscretionary payments fall unevenly across the year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for setting HCE threshold (percentile approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the HCE total compensation amount equal to the annualized weekly earnings of the 85th percentile of full-time salaried workers nationwide (resulting in $151,164 using 2023 data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejected repeating the 2019 (80th percentile) methodology because it would not sufficiently reserve the HCE test for the top of the economic ladder and could risk unintended exemptions in high-wage regions. The Department considered and weighed higher percentiles (e.g., 90th) but judged them potentially unduly restrictive for employers in lower-wage regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from total annual compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Total annual compensation does not include board, lodging, or other facilities, and does not include payments for medical insurance, life insurance, retirement plans, or other fringe benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed components of total annual compensation include commissions, nondiscretionary bonuses, and other nondiscretionary compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Updating mechanism for earnings thresholds (§541.607)
rubrics_metrics.description: Department will update the standard salary level and HCE total compensation requirement initially on July 1, 2024 and every 3 years thereafter to reflect current earnings data, in accordance with the methodology used to set each threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The triennial updates operate independently and sensibly even if other provisions are stayed or invalidated. If the new methodologies are invalidated, the updating provision uses the existing 2019 methodologies as the baseline for future updates (e.g., 20th percentile of weekly earnings in the lowest-wage Census Region and/or retail nationally for the standard salary level; 80th percentile nationally for the HCE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability of provisions (§541.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any provision of part 541 is held invalid or unenforceable (in whole or as applied), the Department intends that the provision be given the fullest effect permitted by law and that the remaining provisions remain effective and operative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department finalized explicit severability text stating each provision is separate and severable and should be construed to continue to give maximum effect permitted by law. The preamble provides examples (e.g., updating mechanism effective even if salary increase invalidated; HCE increase effective even if standard salary increase invalidated) to demonstrate how provisions can operate independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating affected-worker counts requires combined earnings + duties analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining which workers will be affected by a change in the salary level requires examination of workers' earnings and their duties; counting all workers earning below a salary level without considering duties overestimates impacted workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters' claims that all workers earning below a new salary level would be affected failed to account for millions already nonexempt because they fail the duties test. The Department's affected-worker estimates apply probability codes to earnings and duties data and have been used consistently in recent rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: HCE test policy objective (reserve for top earners)
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCE test's primary purpose is to serve as a streamlined alternative for very highly compensated employees because a very high level of compensation is a strong indicator of an employee's exempt status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To serve that purpose the HCE threshold must be high enough to exclude nearly all employees whose EAP status may be questionable; the Department accepts that rare instances may exempt employees who fail duties tests but considers such outcomes acceptable if they are infrequent and involve very highly paid employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical context when setting salary/HCE levels
rubrics_metrics.description: It is useful to put any salary level in historical context (e.g., comparing proportions of salaried workers below short test in 1975 vs proportions below proposed level).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, historical comparisons must be evaluated in light of the fact that prior two-test systems could exempt workers earning below the short test via the long test; thus historical percentage comparisons alone do not dictate the appropriate contemporary salary level.
